title: Hyrox could become an Olympic sport
description:
When you think of Hyrox, you might remember of those viral pictures of an athlete pushing through the race even though diarrhoea was running down her legs.

Her name is Joanna Wietrzyk - and in an exclusive interview with the BBC, she’s described the fallout after she won the competition. She and Hyrox have previously apologised. She’s spoken to the BBC now about the online hate she got after the race (we’ve put the link to that interview at the bottom for you).

It catapulted the fitness craze into the spotlight - but now it’s making headlines again, because of its bid to become an Olympic sport. So how has Hyrox got so popular - and does it have a good chance of making it into the Olympics?

BBC Health reporter and Hyrox athlete Annabel Rackham explains why Hyrox is taking off in a big way. BBC journalist Jacob Evans - who has also just done his first ever Hyrox - shares his experience, and explains some of the difficulties the sport could face in its Olympic bid. And sports journalist Emma Sunny tells us what she think this means for the world of sports more widely.

Also — the Olympics has a long history — which including sports that you might not expect. We put Hannah to the test to see if she can guess which sports have made an appearance over the years.

summaryEn: This episode of What in the World explores the rapid rise of HYROX, a popular fitness competition combining running and functional exercises, and its ambition to become an Olympic sport. Featuring host Hannah Gelbart, BBC health reporter Annabel Rackham, and journalist Jacob Evans, the episode discusses HYROX's appeal as an adult sports day alongside the key hurdles in its Olympic bid, such as high participation costs, equipment requirements, and global accessibility limits, while also touching on past viral controversies and unusual Olympic history.
